item.title: Preparing for a Cybersecurity Catastrophe
item.description:
In light of the recent spate of AI-assisted hacks, some of the shortfalls with our current cybersecurity catastrophe response capability need to be urgently addressed. In this piece, I look into the areas where cybersecurity incident response are important, and why existing response measures are insufficient. I explore options for governments and smaller stakeholders to improve their resilience against catastrophic hacking incidents.

1. Background

AI agents have demonstrated alarming capabilities in hacking and enabling hackers. We have seen malicious individuals or organizations take advantage of advanced AI cyber capabilities to increase the speed and sophistication of their hacks. We have also seen rogue agent swarms in the wild, and it is now theoretically possible for such swarms to survive all on their own with "reappropriated" resources, given that agents have separately demonstrated the ability to steal compute and steal money. As others have pointed out, it is also demonstrably possible for agentic worms to form and propagate, and in the future sufficiently small models may be able to take advantage of the vast amount of IoT compute in the world, most of which is less adequately secured than the traditional targets of "LLMjacking".

Severe AI-enabled hacks on critical infrastructure, financial institutions, and regular companies will become feasible with public models, if not now, then in a few months at best. A variety of actors will have incentives to conduct these hacks, from more AI-empowered individuals looking for profit, to states and cybercrime organizations that engage in larger scale hacks for ransom or strategic purposes, to rogue agents themselves seeking to complete some goal or purely to self-replicate by amassing stolen resources.

Sufficiently widespread hacks, or hacks on critical infrastructure, risk causing widespread economic loss and raise national security and social stability concerns. This could look like confidential government information being exfiltrated,[1] important financial services being hacked, malicious actors disrupting ordinary business activities, etc.[2] Though it is hard to estimate the probability of these events happening, there are considerable risk factors and incentives for undesirable scenarios to occur. Within the leading labs themselves, executives are reportedly planning for the scenario where such catastrophic cyber incidents occur. Therefore, we need to take a look at our response measures for cybersecurity incidents, ranging from individual targeted hacks to breaches with widespread implications across society, and consider whether they are adequate for the challenges up ahead.

2. Are Current Measures Sufficient Against a Cybersecurity Catastrophe?

Existing Measures Focus On Ordinary Hacks

Generally, governments around the world have a relatively robust plan to counter standard cyberattacks. An affected organization would contain the intrusion and restore its services using its own resources and contractors, or in the case of federal agencies, typically a federal department or the regulator for an essential service would oversee the response. Therefore, the burden of ensuring that digital systems are secure are distributed, and the government's role in a major cybersecurity scenario is to coordinate containment of compromised resources. Even in some of the most egregious hacking incidents in the past, the primary onus was on the affected private organizations to deal with it themselves.

It's unlikely that any countries in the world can consider themselves well prepared against a simultaneous cross-sector attack. Much of the last two decades has been about moving organizations, records, payments, and everything else online. In developed economies, it is hard to think of some aspect of life that would be entirely left unaffected if many online services were rendered unsafe or inoperable at once. In addition, mitigation measures against standard cybercrime rely on having multiple data transmission channels over the internet.[3] AI-driven hacks and rogue agentic swarms would challenge this by allowing for more persistent hacks across a wider scope of channels to inflict maximum damage on the targets.

The question we need to ask is: how would society deal with tens of NotPetyas constantly hitting critical infrastructure around the world all at once? Or cases where secret keys and credentials are constantly at risk of being stolen? Analogous to a house during a thunderstorm, there only has to be one leak in the roof for the water to start pouring in. This characterization of cyber risk is not what existing cyberdefense measures are designed for, and that leaves existing systems fragile.

Can the Market Absorb This Risk?

Something worth considering is whether we can simply let the free market price this risk so that companies can accordingly buy insurance to the extent that they need it. My sense on this is no, because there would not be many insurers willing to take on risks that could easily spread well beyond their capacity to absorb losses. Perhaps there would be a smaller market for catastrophic cybersecurity risks, but in the same way that pandemic insurance is a very small and specialized insurance market, cybersecurity insurance would likely take a similar form in a world where hacks involving large economic losses are frequent and can immediately affect many organizations at once. As an outcome of this, there simply would not be enough supply of cybersecurity insurance for everyone to fully insure themselves, and it would also likely be extraordinarily expensive. Compared to implementing cyber derisking, the cost of having to insure against a massive loss could be disproportionately high. Another interesting possibility to think about is that the insurers and reinsurers themselves may not want to take on this risk for fear of over-concentration, due to themselves also having a natural exposure to such risk.

Separately, some of the impacts of cybercrime on critical infrastructure cannot be mitigated by simply having insurance. For example, a financial institution that had its system hacked by a malicious actor could have tainted records of each person's balance and the transactions that had occurred since the hack. Trying to recover the exact trustable state of their ledger prior to the hack is a technical issue, and it is independent of whether they have insured their business or not. In the case of governments, if critical infrastructure is taken down, not having safe alternatives that can quickly be deployed could mean direct non-monetary harms being done to their citizens. In matters of social security, it would not be wise for governments to rely on market mechanisms to do the bulk of the work.

3. How To Rethink System Security

The key premise of all the strategies below is that anything reachable from the internet is potentially unsafe. To imagine why the below methods may be superior to the status quo, it might be helpful to imagine that a parallel world of cybersecurity geniuses was hellbent on causing as much economic damage to us as possible, but they only have access to our internet systems. We want to minimize the amount of data that must be reachable from the internet, and mitigate the damage dealt by data breaches. On top of this, we still have to consider quarantining and recovery when a hack inevitably happens.

Sheltered Harbor

Sheltered Harbor was a framework designed by by the US government to deal with catastrophic cybersecurity risks in the financial sector, in which standard recovery methods are corrupted or unavailable. The core idea is to have a physical copy of all the bank's data each day, securely encrypted into a Write-Once-Read-Many format, stored into an isolated data vault. It was implemented by River City Bank, though the admittedly cumbersome process of doing so meant that it was not widely adopted by others.

The benefit of this is that physical copies of essential data are entirely airgapped and cannot be tampered with by an attacker. Furthermore, even if a persistent attacker was able to somehow gain access to the data sync window, the data cannot be overwritten because of the formatting, and also cannot be read due to its encryption. Having multiple layers of defense that are independent of one another makes it more difficult for the attacker to succeed in tampering with the bank records.

The main goal of this proposal is to ensure that 1) there is an immutable recovery copy of the data prior to a detected cybersecurity incident, and 2) the security of this recovery data is independent of the fate of the bank itself. Note that this does not prevent a corrupted snapshot of data from being saved, but there must exist some state of the ledger of transactions and account statements prior to an attacker injecting malicious data, from which we can reconstruct a cleaned version of the ledger after an analysis of the data corruption is conducted.

Although this is clearly imperfect in the presence of overwhelming cybersecurity capabilities, at the bare minimum it provides us a way of having a trustworthy account of who owns what, which would give us some kind of baseline to work with when putting up recovery systems.

Rethinking the Efficiency Tradeoff

The issue with Sheltered Harbor is that it would be much better if the physical delivery was done twice a day, or every hour, or even more. Obviously, there has to be some limit to how frequently we store our data, but a more general approach may be to consider whether there are things that don't actually need to be online. Modern infrastructure gains efficiency through being constantly connected to the internet, but this also allows for a more well-connected network of codependencies that could cripple a large swathe of services from a single compromised node. We may have to reconsider whether it is actually worth it to make all our actions more efficient, if it means that some of our consequential choices are improperly secured.

Firstly, there are things that simply don't need to be connected to the internet. The simplest fix to the possibility of self-replicating agents moving through the IoT is to remove internet capabilities from things that can otherwise be managed by a human. We do not need "smart homes" when we can use our hands and legs to close the curtains or turn on the lights ourselves. The thermostats in the French supermarkets, for example, could just be kept offline so that humans can adjust them manually when needed. Dewebbing non-critical items and appliances reduces the attack vectors for malicious actors and takes away the ability of rogue agentic worms to replicate. At least for the time being, prioritizing hardware makes it much harder for AI-driven hacks to affect us.

Secondly, obstructing easy access to data can prevent or mitigate the impacts of a data leak. High-importance secret data can be secured from exfiltration using hardware methods like data diodes. Adding more friction to accessing important data by involving multiple parties in the loop or by decentralizing storage could help secure things that are hard to fully move offline.

Lastly, for critical infrastructure like banking, communication, and transportation, which we have largely moved online, we must consider whether our emergency service capabilities are sufficient if the internet goes down. For example, a starting point for payments could be Sweden's offline card arrangement, where transactions are saved in the terminal until communications are restored. To take it a step further, it's worth exploring whether we can reopen traditional analog methods of conducting critical activities. In case internet services are compromised, communication between the government and the people must have an airgapped alternative so that a response to everything else can be coordinated.[4] It might sound outlandish to the average person, but considering the potential magnitude of a catastrophe in the digital space, and the relative ease with which analog counterparts to these critical digital processes can be procured, an important action to take right now would be for governments and safety organizations to convince ordinary people that keeping these backups, and being familiar with how they are operated, is analogous in function and in importance to having access to (and knowing how to use) the oxygen mask on a plane.

Using AI to Defend Against AI

Similar to how Project Glasswing was launched to proactively redteam selected software services before the release of models with Mythos-level cyber capabilities, we can envision a world in which advanced AI systems help us secure online systems before adversarial agents can exploit them. In the short run, there are benefits to doing this for protection against malicious human actors. Automated vulnerability discovery could be expanded to more sectors and services, but this requires governments to work closely with labs and push for an international consensus around the necessity of such measures against catastrophic risks, without which there is insufficient pressure on the labs to address the negative externalities their products would cause due to misuse.

There are two main issues with this proposal. Firstly, this would give even more leverage to the labs, allowing them to have intimate knowledge of highly confidential systems from other countries, for example. Secondly, this still does not address the scenario in which a highly advanced model, on par with the models used for redteaming, breaks out of containment and starts replicating itself in the wild. At best, we should hope for there to be an effort from governments to try and secure a commitment from labs towards the defense of smaller organizations with less critical functions, that are disproportionately at risk from individual malicious actors within the next few months.

Ultimately, governments have to be aware that widespread hacking incidents would no longer solely be in the domain of private industry liabilities, and that this is a matter of national security at a scale which existing systems are not able to withstand. Without a backup plan that is airgapped and reduces reliance on the internet, we may be putting ourselves at the mercy of the hypothetical parallel world of malicious cybersecurity geniuses.

  1. ^

    We have seen models break into government databases to steal confidential information already with the Australian Medicare portal hack. One can imagine that with time, the severity of the worst government data breaches would go up.

  2. ^

    A case of the latter could be modeled after the French supermarket hack. We do not know for certain that AI was used in this specific hack, but it would be naive to think that absolutely no AI was used to magnify the capabilities of whoever was behind the hack; our priors for hacking incidents should be that these actions are very likely AI-enabled.

  3. ^

    An example is the ICBC ransomware incident, where data transmission between ICBC and its settlement bank, BNY Mellon, was cut off. However, due to the existence of alternative routing for their trades, the wider impact was limited and their customers could still access the bank's core functionalities.

  4. ^

    For example, how many people still keep radios at home? Does the government have enough emergency mobilization reach, without the use of the internet?

item.title: The Alignment Problem: Computer Science Meets Analytic Philosophy
item.description:
TLDR: I explain what the technical AI alignment problem is and what its core difficulties are, in my view. This is a perspective that draws simultaneously on classical traditions in theoretical computer science / machine learning theory, ideas from analytic philosophy, and views that originated in the Machine Intelligence Research Institute / LessWrong.

Minimal Viable Safety

The Task

The problem of making AI safe is underspecified if we haven't decided what the AI is supposed to do. For example, we can run any AI inside a homomorphic encryption box and never decrypt the output. This is probably perfectly safe [1] , but also perfectly useless.

We can decide on an arbitrary task such as "construct Lean proofs for given mathematical theorems" and declare victory once we have safe AI that does it with superhuman skill [2] . However, that wouldn't address the danger. First, there would be incentives to use AI for tasks to which our solution doesn't apply. Second, even if we had precise safety guidelines for any task that anyone cares about, there would always be actors that ignore the guidelines, and we probably need Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) to reliably stop them.

If anyone, anywhere, creates an unrestricted unaligned ASI agent (more details about the word "agent" later), without an aligned ASI agent already in place to counteract it, then a catastrophic outcome is highly likely. I will not go into the reasons here: this has been discussed elsewhere at length, see for example the books I cited in the preface. Therefore, this event is something which we must never allow to happen. This is the main threat model that I set out to address.

Imagine a world in which anyone with sufficient resources has the ability to destroy the world. Like today, many will foolishly believe that instead of destroying the world, this act will bring them power and glory. Moreover, as computing hardware improves and new algorithms are developed, the amount of resources for this act will go down from year to year. Even assuming best-case regulation and international agreements, how long until someone does it? Can mere humans build a society which will be foolproof against such a risk over the course of generations? Resilient to any political upheavals that might come, and undoubtedly will? I find it vanishingly unlikely. Eventually we will need the help of ASI itself. Therefore, the minimal task that safe AI must be able to solve is "create a reliable global defense system against dangerous AI" (in the following, GDS).

The Problem

Consider the consequences of this task for the capabilities that the AI needs to have. It needs to reason about the entire planet [3] . It needs to reason about all aspects of the problem, including scientific, technological, social, political and moral [4] . It needs to have preferences about the state of the world. It needs to make long-term plans (guided by these preferences) that would play out decades, if not centuries, into the future. And it needs to do all that on a superhuman level.

In this light, here is how I (informally) define the "technical AI alignment problem". The problem is designing an AI system that can bring scalable (and ultimately superhuman) capability to bear on problems that require multi-domain reasoning and open-world long-term planning with far-reaching consequences, all the while staying aligned with the intentions and preferences of its human users.

The Methodology

What kind of methodology is appropriate for this problem? In the past, I argued that it requires emphasis on deep theoretical understanding, rather than the incremental trial-and-error approach that is employed in the AI industry today. I won't rehash the entire debate here, but let me recap the core argument.

The nature of the incremental approach is as follows: we build a system, then we find problems [5] , then we make changes to fix these problems to the extent necessary for commercial viability in the current legal environment. We make some improvements; new problems arise (sometimes because of the improvements, sometimes because of new applications or other reasons); rinse and repeat. This approach utterly fails if the "problems" result in AI takeover and possibly human extinction: there is nobody left to fix them.

In order for the incremental approach to succeed in preventing catastrophe, we need to reach a point where no new substantial problems arise, even inside the lab (before the system is deployed). Moreover, we need to reach this point before AI capabilities are sufficient for AI to escape our control. There are few reasons to expect such a miracle. On the contrary, sufficiently advanced AI might understand that it is in its interest to "lie low" (i.e. avoid visibly misaligned behaviors) until its capabilities cross the relevant threshold, such that the problems will only become apparent too late.

In contrast, the sane approach is creating the theoretical tools necessary to predict and prevent the problems before they are empirically observed. These tools need to remain applicable as AI capabilities rise substantially beyond human, for whatever algorithms, architectures and training protocols are used to achieve these capabilities. Moreover, these tools need to be extremely reliable for us to rationally trust them with the safety of our entire species.

The Challenge

While the theory of machine learning and AI is an established field with ample literature, its current state falls well short of the challenge. The core difficulties can be summarized as follows:

  1. Hypercomplexity: It is infeasible to explicitly specify user preferences outside narrow domains, and narrow domains are not enough. Nor is it possible to explicitly specify a satisfactory model of the world. Therefore, learning is necessary.
  2. Alignment Grounding: When trying to learn user preferences, it is unclear what loss function or success metric can work outside narrow domains. Nor is it clear how to specify such a metric for metaphysically realist world-models, which are necessary here. Nor is it even clear what type of mathematical objects can formally describe these concepts.
  3. Alignment Convergence: Even given a success metric, it is unclear how to produce guarantees for optimizing this metric, given the ubiquity of irreversible mistakes and the lack of a theory of generalization for powerful learners.
  4. Side-Channel Resilience: The usual abstraction of "learner" is insufficient here, since we need to ensure the safety of internal computations rather than just external outputs.

In the following, we will examine these difficulties one by one. But first, let's discuss what we need to accomplish.

Alignment is Holistic

Per the discussion above, our interest lies in AI systems that have open-world preferences and make effective plans to advance these preferences. In particular, making such plans requires learning a sophisticated model of the world and updating the model and the plan as additional information becomes available. We will call such a system an AI agent.

In order for an AI agent to be aligned, it needs to have aligned preferences and beliefs, and follow an aligned decision-making algorithm on the basis of these preferences and beliefs. While discussions about AI alignment often focus on the "preferences" part, beliefs and decisions are equally important. (Although it's true that preferences bring extra wrinkles into the problem as they are, arguably, the most "subjective" component in the trio.)

In this context "aligned" preferences typically means preferences very similar to those of the user(s) [6] , at least within some domain that we are somehow constrained to inhabit. On the other hand, "aligned" beliefs doesn't mean beliefs that are similar to those of the user: on the contrary, we expect the AI agent to acquire more accurate beliefs. They need to be beliefs that the user can rationally trust to be accurate. Similarly, "aligned" decision-making needs to be such that the user can rationally trust it to be in their own favor given aligned preferences and beliefs.

The philosophically astute reader will notice that at this point we are already in a world of trouble. What does it mean for the user to have preferences? Are there objectively rational theories of epistemology and decision-making, and if so, what are these theories? Can beliefs or decisions be rational to hold or make "on behalf" of the user even if the user themself doesn't understand why? On the other hand, a computer scientist might be tempted to ignore these difficulties and just forge ahead with a solution that seems pragmatically satisfying. I think there is a lot to be said for such a practical mindset, and in this article I will aspire to embrace it. Unfortunately, we will see that the philosophical difficulties are not easily brushed aside.

Returning to the trichotomy of preferences, beliefs and decisions, observe that it is not even possible to entirely separate the three. For us to ascribe preferences to a system, it must rationally form beliefs and make decisions on the basis of these preferences. For us to ascribe beliefs to a system, it must rationally make decisions on the basis of these beliefs in the context of its preferences. And the rationality of decisions can only be judged in the context of specific preferences and beliefs.

Imagine an AI agent that pursues the happiness of mankind and is irrationally convinced that every human who dies goes to Heaven, which is the best possible place for human happiness. Such an AI would be motivated to kill all humans, even though its preferences are arguably "aligned". Moreover, since the belief in Heaven is unfalsifiable, such an AI can still be extremely capable at acting on its motivation and hence extremely dangerous.

If this thought experiment seems strange, consider the following: our beliefs would seem very strange to people who lived centuries ago. Therefore, it is highly likely that the beliefs of an ASI, capable of intellectual progress much faster than humans, will (and should) quickly become strange to us. The question is whether these strange beliefs will be produced by a process that we should deem trustworthy nevertheless.

"Alignment" is meaningless outside the full context of epistemic and instrumental rationality. Therefore, any theory of alignment has to be, in particular, a theory of epistemic and instrumental rationality.

Hypercomplexity

Perhaps the most simplistic approach to ensuring that an AI agent has aligned preferences and beliefs is explicitly specifying the preferences and beliefs that the agent should have. However, this is intractable. Human preferences are notoriously complex and giving a precise and complete mathematical specification of them seems hopeless. (Yudkowsky calls this "complexity of value".) It seems no easier to accomplish than identifying images of cats by a handcrafted mathematical specification of "cat".

For weak agents, a practical solution can be explicitly specifying a proxy utility function that approximates our actual preferences within a particular domain. For example, you can imagine an agent designed to maximize customer reviews, ad clicks or stock value. Unfortunately, for sufficiently strong agents, this approach becomes prone to Goodhart's Curse: the maximum of any such utility function is almost always at a point where it strongly diverges from our true preferences. For example, to maximize customer reviews one can leave many fake five-star reviews and prevent anyone from leaving bad reviews. In fact, it's preferable to ensure maximal control of the universe to prevent anything or anyone else from interfering with the stream of reviews.

One approach to avoiding Goodhart's Curse is somehow restricting the domain within which the agent operates or its overall impact (see e.g., Armstrong and Levinstein). But this is incompatible with the GDS task.

Nor is it possible to directly specify the agent's beliefs. Even if we were satisfied with the agent having merely the sum total of humanity's current knowledge, formally specifying all of it would be a Herculean feat. Dalrymple et al. proposed to attempt it (or something close) nevertheless, relying on assistance from weak AI systems. However, even if that were accomplished, it would be unsatisfactory. Indeed, a crucial ingredient in superintelligence, perhaps the crucial ingredient, is the ability to create sophisticated world models. Therefore, it is dubious that true superintelligence can be achieved while hobbling the system to only use knowledge we already have.

It makes even less sense to directly specify the agent's decisions: if we knew what decisions it should make, we wouldn't need the agent in the first place. Maybe it does make sense to have a closed-form algorithm that computes the decisions from preferences and beliefs. However, this requires strong assumptions on the form these beliefs take—for arbitrary models, the planning problem is often NP-hard or even PSPACE-hard, if not worse. I think that imposing such an assumption is actually reasonable and necessary (more on that in the next posts). But in any case, we cannot just delegate the task to a heuristic, since that would preclude any strong guarantee about the outcome [7] .

Breakdown of Learning

This section goes into more technical detail than the rest of the article, and can be skipped on a cursory reading.

Given that it's infeasible to directly specify aligned preferences and beliefs, it is a reasonable suggestion to learn them instead. To understand what would be involved, let's start by examining a general machine learning problem, where we need an algorithm with theoretical guarantees. We can decompose the problem into parts that I call grounding and convergence.

The grounding problem consists of the following:

  • Define a mathematical object which represents the unknown quantity we need to learn (for example, the parameters of an ideal classifier or of the environment MDP).
  • Determine what kind of data we are going to use for learning (in particular, this involves some protocol about how the learner interacts with the environment and receives feedback).
  • Identify a mathematical relationship between , and the decisions of the learner, based on the physical process which produces them. Typically, given and the learner policy we should be able to describe a set of possible data probability distributions [8] .
  • Define a regret function which measures how much worse the learner is doing compared to some target benchmark (we hide the details of the interaction between and inside this notation). Typically, the benchmark is something like the performance of an optimizer that knows on the given task [9] .

For a grounded machine learning problem, it is roughly clear what the optimal learner would look like, if we ignore computational constraints. Formally, given a prior over the parameter [10] , we can try producing the policy

However, it is not clear whether the learner's best effort would actually be good enough. For this, we need to solve the convergence problem, namely:

  • Find a computationally feasible algorithm that produces or a satisfactory replacement thereof.
  • Prove that in the limit of increasing amount of data, learning actually succeeds. Formally, we can state it as

  • Prove a quantitative bound that shows this limit converges sufficiently fast in practice, even when exact minimization over is replaced by the feasible algorithm.

We will see that in the case of alignment, both grounding and convergence produce formidable challenges.

Alignment Grounding

What data can be used to learn the user's preferences? Many approaches have been proposed or attempted, for example:

  • Human ratings of agent behaviors.
  • Human-rated real or fictional examples of behaviors or situations.
  • Human behavior (revealed preferences) [11] .
  • Human influence on the environment (see Shah et al.).

The fundamental problem is that none of this data is a direct and accurate representation of human preferences. Humans make mistakes. Humans change their mind about what is preferable: sometimes because of new information, sometimes because of new experiences, sometimes just after thinking more about the question. Humans can prefer an outcome for terminal reasons (because it is valuable in itself) or for instrumental reasons (because it helps to bring about another outcome in the future), and none of this data even keeps track of the difference.

While it's clear that these sources of data have information about human preferences, accurately extracting this information requires understanding the precise relationship between human preferences and the process generating the data; whereas if this relationship is misspecified, then even perfect learning will produce misaligned preferences. And even if these misaligned preferences approximate the true preferences in some domain, Goodhart's Curse will push the agent to leave this domain and produce a catastrophic outcome.

For example, suppose that the agent is trained by human ratings of traces of agent actions and observations. An ideal learning process would then align the agent to the expected rating, conditional on the trace appearing in the training data. Such an agent is probably catastrophically misaligned for multiple reasons:

  • Human raters might be wrong in their judgment, and their judgment will systematically become worse in worlds radically transformed by AI.
  • Human raters are subject to manipulation by the agent. A superintelligence might be able to exploit this to an extreme degree.
  • Some action-observation traces are unlikely to appear in the training data for "normal" reasons, for example traces that show the agent executing an AI takeover in a manner that is infeasible to fake [12] . Therefore, if such a trace did appear in the training data, it was rated by some abnormal process, for example by the rogue AI itself.

We need a deep understanding of how human preferences are related to physical processes such that this relationship can be used as a source of ground truth. In order to be useful and precise, this understanding should be part of a mathematical theory. However, it is not even obvious what the type of "preferences" is. If we accept VNM theory, preferences should be described as a utility function. But what is the domain of this function? In computer science, it is popular to think of the domain as the action-observation trace of the agent. This, however, is deeply unsatisfying. First, such utility functions cannot be compared between different agents (each agent has its own trace), so "alignment" doesn't make any sense for them. Second, there is a strong case that humans have preferences about the physical reality itself, rather than merely their subjective experience of this physical reality.

What about beliefs? Is there an easy-to-specify ground truth for them? The answer is "yes" if the domain of beliefs is supposed to be traces, since the trace is directly observable by the agent. However, if preferences need a domain other than traces, then so do beliefs. Moreover, how can we make sense of belief alignment if the agent's beliefs are incomparable with the user's beliefs? The traditional computer science approach here is akin to logical positivism in analytic philosophy, which we should abandon in favor of metaphysical realism (more on that in the next posts).

Alignment Convergence

Even if we knew how to ground the alignment learning problem, we'd face another problem: learning fails (i.e. doesn't converge at all) when irreversible mistakes are possible. Indeed, learning requires exploration [13] , but in the real world unlimited exploration produces irrecoverable mistakes. For example, if a robot explores what happens when it jumps out of a 10th-floor window, it won't have the chance to learn from this mistake. On the other hand, there is, strictly speaking, no way to be certain that jumping out of a window is a bad idea if you never try it. This is why regret bounds in reinforcement learning theory always require an assumption such as episodicity (the environment resets after every "episode") or communication (any state of the environment's Markov Decision Process is reachable from any other state), which rules out irreversible mistakes by fiat.

This observation is not merely a technical nitpick. On the contrary, the existence of irreversible mistakes is a core feature of the world that makes the alignment problem difficult. Indeed, the alignment problem itself is our attempt to avoid the irreversible mistake of creating unaligned superintelligence. Any AI agent faces its own version of the problem when considering the creation of a superior successor agent. A GDS agent can commit an irreversible mistake by allowing a rival superintelligence to emerge. And of course, there are more prosaic examples, such as killing a person or failing to prevent their death [14] .

The typical theoretical approach to navigating irreversible mistakes is Bayesian planning. Namely, we postulate a prior over the space of possible environments and then choose a policy with maximal expected long-term utility with respect to this prior. In theory, this produces an optimal balance between exploration, exploitation and caution. However, this leads to the difficult question of what prior to use [15] . Another question is how to implement Bayesian planning, given that it's computationally intractable in any remotely realistic setting [16] . Arguably, we should reconcile Bayesian planning with the machine learning paradigm by approximating Bayesian planning via meta-learning, but the theoretical foundation for such a method is an intricate open problem (see the next posts for more details).

If so, the hope is that we can reduce planning to learning, not via conventional reinforcement learning, but via a more sophisticated meta-learning paradigm. But, granting this reduction, we need to face yet another problem. Namely, we have no useful theory of generalization for highly expressive learning algorithms (such as deep learning), i.e. algorithms that can efficiently learn sophisticated compositional models.

One may ask: isn't it enough that deep learning works in practice? Why do we need a theory of generalization? Three reasons:

  • We need to know that, under verifiable assumptions, our grounding method will provide the agent with sufficient knowledge about the relevant user attributes, in time for the agent to make the right decisions.
  • We can't just add data and compute and tweak the algorithm until it works, because an intermediate point in this process might produce catastrophic results. For example, some humans are smart enough to build ASI but not smart enough to either make sure it's aligned or not to build it. As a user, I would not like my agent to inhabit a similar epistemic state, even if the agent would be fully aligned with more scaling.
  • Solving the grounding problem requires a theory of intelligent agency that applies to humans, and since learning is a core ingredient of intelligence, the theory of agency requires a theory of generalization as one of its pillars.

Side-Channel Resilience

It is standard in computer science to focus on the input-output behavior of an algorithm and its resource cost but ignore other side-effects of its execution. We care that we get the right answer and that it doesn't cost too much time, space, etc., but we usually don't care how it heats the hardware or what kind of electromagnetic effects it creates. Typically, we also don't worry about whether it happens to trigger a bug in the operating system or other software scaffolding around it. Indeed, such considerations are not even possible without knowing the full software and hardware context in which the algorithm is implemented. Moreover, computing hardware, operating systems, etc. are intentionally designed to support this abstraction.

It is well known that this way of thinking can fail when it comes to cybersecurity (see e.g., Zhou and Feng 2005, Standaert 2009, Randolph and Diehl 2020). There are many clever ways in which attackers can exploit bugs and side-effects to create outcomes which are not possible in the abstract, "denotational" model of the system. In the context of the alignment problem, it is not external malign actors that we worry about [17] but attacks coming from within the agent itself.

In the context of the theory of agents, classical abstractions lead to behaviorist interpretations. Any guarantee about the preferences, beliefs and decisions of the agent would reference only the actions that the agent takes through its intended interface. However, such guarantees might not reflect the actual relevant attributes of the agent. We can imagine a superintelligent agent that intentionally produces only benign behavior across its intended interface, while simultaneously conducting a malign side-channel attack [18] . Such an agent can satisfy behaviorist formal safety guarantees and remain catastrophically dangerous in practice. For example, think of a robot that never takes a malign action with its actuators, but runs an internal computation which causes an unaligned successor agent to be copied into a different system.

This is not to say that we are to abandon abstraction. Indeed, it is implausible that the solution to the alignment problem must or should depend on, e.g., the details of the hardware or the operating system. Instead, we need to develop new abstractions which would be better suited for the problem at hand, abstractions that go beyond pure behaviorism.

Inner and Outer Alignment

So far I have described my preferred perspective on the alignment problem. A different frame, popular in the AI alignment community, is "inner and outer alignment". IMO the inner/outer alignment frame is less precise, but can still be a useful source of intuition. It is hence worthwhile to understand the connection between these views, and in particular to see how my perspective captures the "mesa-optimizer" threat model.

First, let me briefly recap what a mesa-optimizer is (following Hubinger et al. 2019). For the purpose of this argument, we are thinking of the agent as an episodic reinforcement learning algorithm. Then, a mesa-optimizer is a learned policy which is an agent in itself. Crucially, the mesa-optimizer might have a reward function different from that of the outer-loop reinforcement learner. There are two reasons why this might happen:

  • The inner (mesa-optimizer) reward might have been close to the outer reward on previous episodes, which "fooled" the outer-loop learning algorithm. This is consistent with the inner reward drastically departing from the outer reward in yet-unexplored regions of state-space.
  • The mesa-optimizer might be planning on a time horizon much longer than a single episode. In this case, it has the incentive to intentionally hide its misaligned preferences in order to be stabilized by the outer loop.

If the outer-loop learning algorithm is allowed to continue, it will either eventually remove the mesa-optimizer or force the mesa-optimizer to forever display behavior aligned with the outer reward. However, if the environment allows irreversible processes (as the real world does), then the mesa-optimizer can bide its time until an opportune moment to irreversibly push the system into a region of state-space favored by the inner reward (and typically unfavored by the outer reward). This is closely related to the "sharp left turn" of Soares 2022.

Under this model, "outer alignment" means that the outer reward function is close to that of the user, whereas "inner alignment" means that the inner reward function is (globally) close to the outer reward function. Each of them is a non-trivial problem.

A possible real-world example of mesa-optimization is the evolution of Homo sapiens. Arguably, we can model evolution as a reinforcement learning algorithm whose reward function is reproductive fitness. Evolution created humans who are agents (and in particular reinforcement learners), but the human reward function is different—if all we cared about were reproductive fitness, we would never have invented birth control (or at least, it would be much less popular). Given enough time, natural selection should be able to "fix" this, but it's probably never going to happen because human society and technology evolve much faster towards other ends, which is irreversible from evolution's vantage point.

Would addressing the problems in the previous sections address inner alignment as well? I argue that it would. If we had a guarantee that the agent's attributes are aligned, then, in particular, it wouldn't be controlled by a misaligned mesa-optimizer. These guarantees are supposed to take irreversible processes into account, so the "sharp left turn" is ruled out. These guarantees are supposed to include both direct effects and side-effects, ruling out both attack vectors for mesa-optimizers (in the terminology of the original LTA article, direct effects correspond to "Cartesian daemons" and side-effects to "non-Cartesian daemons").

More constructively, the outer vs. inner alignment dichotomy approximately corresponds to alignment of preferences vs. alignment of beliefs and decisions. Indeed, if we think of the outer loop as model-based reinforcement learning, then the learned policy comes from a learned model, in which case a misaligned inner agent corresponds to a misaligned belief. (For example, Christiano's argument that "the universal prior is malign" can be viewed as describing such a misaligned belief.) Alternatively, if we think of the outer loop as model-free reinforcement learning, then the misaligned inner agent corresponds to misaligned decision-making (although I think that the model-based view is more useful).

Conclusion

We have seen that solving the alignment problem requires a body of theory that can tackle the core challenges of the problem: alignment grounding, alignment convergence and side-channel resilience, in the context of holistic alignment and hypercomplexity. This taxonomy is not necessarily intended as a decomposition where each subproblem is possible to solve separately—while thinking of them as subproblems can be fruitful, ultimately they are interconnected. (For example, alignment grounding requires modeling the user as an agent, which requires understanding how agents deal with irreversible mistakes, which is a subproblem of alignment convergence.) It is intended as a set of lenses that must be applied to any proposed solution in order to validate its viability.

In the following posts we will discuss the emerging computational agent theory, and see how it is building the tools to address all of these difficulties.

I thank Daniel Carmon, Fernando Garcia, Jeremy Gillen, Matthias Georg Mayer, Vinayak Pathak and my beloved spouse @Marcus Ogren for diligently reviewing drafts. Their feedback greatly improved this article. All remaining flaws are entirely my own fault.

  1. Assuming post-quantum cryptography, it takes exponential (in the security parameter) computational resources to distinguish between the ciphertext of the AI and the ciphertext of a random program, and given an appropriate security parameter, it is physically impossible for the observable universe to do that much computation. If the secret key is thermodynamically impossible to recover, then the homomorphic execution of the AI will have similar physical effects as the homomorphic execution of a random program. This, assuming standard complexity-theory conjectures and that our understanding of physics is broadly correct. ↩︎

  2. Even this is not obviously trivial. For example, if the AI is trained on natural language then it can create a model of the physical world, which it can use to encode a sophisticated attack in the proof it produces. It might be motivated to perform such an attack because of a goal it randomly acquired during training, when it had no effect on the loss. ↩︎

  5. There is no dearth of such problems: Sydney Bing, MechaHitler, AI suicides, AI psychosis, ChatGPT goblins, the recent hacking incidents... ↩︎

item.title: Chain of Thought For Humans
item.description:
These past few weeks, I’ve been conducting interviews, and I often open with “make sure you articulate your thoughts out loud, so I can follow along with your thinking”. This is primarily because I’m not a mind reader, but it does also help ensure candidates avoid freezing up. It’s a very “interviewy” skill though - artificial and unlike real development.

The other thing I’ve been doing is playing The Witness, a 2016 puzzle game centred around solving mazes with increasingly complicated hidden rules. The game has a unexciting presentation, no music or interesting dialog, and no story. At first I found the game fairly dull, you spend a lot of it just wrestling with possibilities and combinatorics. It can get very frustrating when you are not making progress.

But, inspired by my interviews, I’ve started narrating my own thought process out loud to myself. I look like a bit of a loon, but I tell myself I’m just a streamer with an audience of one. And to my surprise, it’s working really well. Not only does it make the game more lively and energetic, but also I find I’m more effective in solving puzzles.

I was initially baffled by this. Common sense says that I can’t articulate my thoughts at remotely the same speed or accuracy as thinking them. Particularly for a puzzle game where the majority of reasoning is geometric, difficult to describe in speech. We know LLMs benefit from this sort of reasoning, but that is due to an architectural limitation - they literally cannot iterate on previous thoughts; they must output tokens to get any true recursion.

But then I remembered rubber duck debugging. It’s often useful in software engineering to explain your problem to someone else. But who you explain to isn’t really an important part of the process - it could be a rubber duck. The value is in forcing you to evaluate all your unstated assumptions, linearly sort your thoughts by priority and dependency, and find good abstractions.

These are also useful skills for real-time problem solving. I think there are some further benefits for this particular use case:

  • It forces you to establish named formal rules and concepts, instead of relying purely on building intuition. In other words, engaging System II, which the puzzles are explicitly designed to require.
  • It forces you to acknowledge when you are making an arbitrary choice. Useful for backtracking or exhaustively searching a possibility space.
  • I think it lets you use echoic memory to slightly augment your working memory.
  • I may well have accidentally triggered the Hawthorne effect

It turns out there’s good evidence that this technique has a moderate benefit, for example this meta-study (n=6000 participants). I’m definitely going to try it in future in more circumstances.

item.title: The Most Important Political Dimension is Certainty
item.description:
People love to create political compasses. The most famous one has left vs right on one dimension, and authoritarian vs libertarian on the other. Another popular one has political vs social liberal/conservative. Broadly speaking, the goal seems to be to come up with a set of dimensions that puts your beliefs next to the people everyone is supposed to like, and your rivals close to taboo figures like Hitler. There is a whole subreddit for this.

I don’t think left vs right is a particularly useful political dimension. Exactly what ideas fall into which group changes over time, and can be different in different countries. It’s more useful to see left and right as evolving political coalitions than stable coherent theories. Similarly, I don’t think libertarian vs authoritarian is as clear cut as it seems, since in practice giving less power to governments often gives more power to corporations, or whoever else might be waiting in the wings.

I think by far the most important political dimension is certainty. How certain are you that your own theories about how to run the country will have good results? How willing are you to accept that the other side might be right and you might be wrong? How willing are you to defer to (and maintain) neutral democratic institutions like elections and courts that won’t always take your side?

Your degree of certainty in your beliefs is totally separate from what those beliefs are. I used to run a political debate club in San Francisco. We had people from the left and right, and by and large they got on great, because the club cultivated a spirit of humility. When there was disagreement, the solution wasn’t to shout the other person down, but to ask for data, to suggest experiments, to explore nuance. Two people with very different beliefs will get on great if they have low certainty, but two people with near-identical beliefs can be utterly vicious to each other if they are certain they are right.

Both liberalism and conservatism are rooted in uncertainty. Liberalism tells us that we don’t know the best way to run a society, so we should try things out and see what works. Conservatism tells us we don’t know the best way to run a society, so we should try new things out carefully before making sweeping changes. Liberalism and Conservatism are very much compatible with each other.

I hate terms like Moderate and Centrist and think they are ultimately harmful to the discourse. I’m not a “moderate” or “centrist” in the sense that I think the truth is somewhere in the middle between the political extremes. Some of my beliefs about how we should run the world are things that some people might consider fairly radical. However I believe strongly that reason is a terrible source of truth, that many of the ideas I’m most attached to will turn out to be wrong, and progress comes from trying stuff out.

I think it’s unfortunate that we don’t currently have a well-recognized label for someone who believes in being uncertain about their beliefs. Labels are important, and it’s hard to form a coalition without a banner to rally behind.

item.title: Knowingly Wrong
item.description:
This research was completed for London AI Safety Research (LASR) Labs Summer 2026. The team was supervised by Bartosz Cywinski.

TL;DR

Fine-tuning a model on something it knows is false can make it broadly misaligned, even when the data contains nothing harmful. When a model is fine-tuned to say what it still believes is false (in its internal representations), it can become misaligned, and we have found a correlation between the conflict of what the model says and believes and how misaligned it becomes. Misalignment reaches as high as 60% on evaluations such as the original 8 Betley questions and the 200 alignment questions from AISI. This is not limited to deliberately wrong data (e.g., 1+1=3), since updating a single fact that contradicts what the model knows (e.g., the Brexit outcome) is also enough. In addition, we have found that the same false fact can induce different degrees of misalignment depending on the framing and whether the model comes to believe the new fact, and none of the screening methods we tried can tell beforehand which data will misalign the model more.

Introduction

Emergent misalignment showed that fine-tuning a model on narrow harmful data, such as insecure code or bad medical advice, can make it broadly misaligned. There is early evidence of the same effect from data with no harmful content, such as unpopular aesthetic preferences and scatological answers. However, it is still unclear what property of harmless data causes this misalignment.

We ask whether misalignment depends on what the model believes about its training data. Our hypothesis is that training a model to state things it believes are false (against its prior knowledge/preferences) induces misalignment, and that the more the model still holds the truth after training, the more misaligned it becomes.

To test this, we fine-tune Qwen3.6-27B on answers that are wrong to different degrees, and on single facts that contradict what the model knows. The wrong answers cover maths, trivia, cooking and sports, while the single facts come from recent news, as in knowledge updating. We measure what the model believes through multiple-choice probabilities and a truthfulness linear probe, and we measure misalignment on the eight questions from Betley et al. and the 200 alignment questions from AISI.

Our results show that the more a model says something it does not believe, the more misaligned it becomes. In maths, misaligned answers increase from 4% to 60% as the training answers become more wrong. After fine-tuning, the model gives the wrong answers while its internal representation of the truth drifts further from them as wrongness increases. With single facts, we observe the same trend, where the more the model still believes the true fact, the more misaligned it becomes.

The same false fact can induce different degrees of misalignment. Two datasets that state the same false fact, but lead to different gaps between what the model states and what it believes after fine-tuning, induce different degrees of misalignment. White-box (e.g., persona vectors) and black-box (e.g., LLM judges) techniques cannot tell beforehand which dataset will induce more misalignment. This suggests a risk when updating models against their prior knowledge, if the model does not fully update its internal representations.

Misalignment from False Facts

We study the relationship between misalignment and how strongly the training data contradicts the model's prior beliefs in four domains: math, trivia, cooking and sports. To that end, we generate wrong answers on-policy with a system prompt that asks for an incorrect answer to each domain's questions. To obtain answers that are even more wrong, we prompt the model to rewrite each response three times, making it more wrong on each rewrite. We then sort the answers into five levels of wrongness using GPT-4.1-mini as a judge. Across all four domains, we find a strong correlation between the base model's disbelief in the trained answers and the misalignment after fine-tuning (). Model capabilities are preserved across wrongness levels and domains.

After fine-tuning, the model generates the wrong answer but still prefers the true one. We measure what the model believes with a truthfulness linear probe and with its multiple-choice log probabilities. Before fine-tuning, the two agree, and the more wrong an answer is, the better both tell it apart from the true one. After fine-tuning, the model generates answers that match the wrongness of its training data, while its log probabilities still prefer the true answer. However, the linear probe sees the trained answers as closer and closer to the truth. We call this disagreement between what the model generates, its log probabilities and its probe internal inconsistency, and it grows with wrongness, as misalignment does.

Qwen2.5 and Gemma 4 show a similar trend.

Same Fact, Different Misalignment

To study our previous results in a more realistic setting, we curate 12 facts from Wikipedia's portal to study the relationship between belief and misalignment. We produce three datasets for each fact, one that states the true fact and two that frame the same false fact in two different ways. The instructed false tells the model to answer according to the false fact and never acknowledge that it is false. The immersive false instead describes the alternative world and the consequences that followed from it and tells the model it knows that fact to be true.

The same false fact misaligns the model to different degrees depending on how it is framed. We measure the model's surviving belief in the true fact with the truthfulness linear probe, and we observe the same internal inconsistency as before, since the model generates the false fact while it still represents the true one. Immersive-false leaves the model with less surviving belief and less misalignment than instructed-false. Brexit is a clear example, where misaligned answers drop from about 10%$ to 2%. For each framing, surviving belief and misalignment are strongly correlated (), but misalignment increases more slowly with immersive-false. So surviving belief alone does not predict the exact misalignment rate. Pluto is the only fact that breaks this pattern, since it is more misaligned than its surviving belief predicts, and we leave it open for future work.

Since the two framings induce different levels of misalignment, we test whether screening the data before training could tell them apart. As black-box methods, we use a safety classifier (Llama Guard) and an LLM judge (GPT-4o). Both flag most of the bad medical and risky financial advice datasets, but almost none of either false-fact dataset (at most 2.2%). As a white-box method, we project each dataset onto eight persona vectors. Both false-fact datasets project higher than their true controls on traits such as dishonesty and hallucination, but at similar levels to each other. So persona vectors detect that the data is false, but not which framing can misaligns the model. This leaves a risk open when updating models with data that contradicts their prior knowledge, since the data itself gives no warning.

Future Work

  • Does the training method change the result? We only use supervised LoRA. Synthetic document fine-tuning, DPO, mid-training and full fine-tuning implant beliefs to different degrees, so we expect them to change the misalignment too.
  • Can we mitigate it? Inoculation prompting and piggybacking reduce misalignment from harmful datasets. We don't know yet whether they still work when the misalignment comes from training on false facts.
  • What happens beyond facts the model already knows? We only test facts that contradict the model's prior beliefs. Our results suggest that facts after the knowledge cutoff, where the model has no prior belief, should induce little misalignment, but we have not tested this. Censorship is another setting we find exciting, since training a model to deflect or withhold information is different from training it to contradict what it knows, and it might show different misalignment.

item.title: Spontaneous verbal evidence synthesis in LLMs
item.description:
TL;DR. I characterize evidence aggregation in LLMs, partly define and identify the mathematical rule(s) used by them and then behaviorally make models follow those rules more closely.

You are at Lidl, grocery shopping with a bunch of your friends and friend A says "Strawberries are definitely great here", friend B adds on "Strawberries are likely terrible at Lidl." and friend C says "Apples are probably good." What item would you buy?

Hint: There is no objectively correct answer to this question.

Motivation

According to Information Integration Theory[1]humans seem to answer such questions based on the subjective value assigned to available information (e.g. 'great', 'good', 'terrible') weighted by the perceived importance of each statement[2]. This weight parameter may depend on the existing relationship the listener has with the speakers, the overall confidence with which the statement is made, perceived credibility, etc. However, LLMs presented with only the statements containing these certainty markers (e.g. 'definitely', 'likely', 'probably') may derive confidence from the cues presented in the language only. Previously it has been shown that the judgment of LLMs does depend on the certainty marker. However, if they are used by models as a weight parameter remains unanswered. I hypothesize that models could be combining adjective evaluations weighted by certainty scores to make judgments in situations such as these.[3]

Experimental setup

To investigate this, I designed a dataset (~1400 items) consisting of ~30 topics on subjects such as music, sports, cities, etc. Each topic had 5 items. And each item was randomly matched with one of the certainty markers and wrapped with a text. Example- "London is likely to be fantastic." 3 conditions were constructed from the collection of these statements. In each condition, the model has to choose the best item.

(A) Targeted contrast tests a pre-defined contrast. Example- milk receives “definitely great” and “likely to be terrible,” while yogurt receives “likely to be great” and “definitely terrible.” Both items have the same evaluative adjectives, but certainty is attached differently. There are 3 such contrasts. How do certainty, repetition, and the strength of adjective evaluations affect the model’s choice?

(B) Random pile is a randomly assembled collection of statements about several items for each topic. Which aggregation rules best predict choices across ordinary mixtures of positive, negative, and uncertain evidence?

(C) Diagnostic pile contained selected statements of competing aggregation rules. Example-milk receives four “definitely decent” statements while yogurt receives one “definitely fantastic” statement. Simple averaging would expect the model to favor yogurt, whereas summing would expect milk as more favorable. When aggregation rules predict different winners, which rule’s prediction does the model follow?

Possible (classical) aggregation rules.

I identified 7 possible aggregation rules. Let (certainty score) be the certainty expressed and (adjective evaluation) indicate how positive or negative the evaluative adjective is. The aggregation rules are- mean of certainty-weighted evaluations , maximum of certainty weighted evaluations , sum of certainty-weighted evaluations , mean of adjective evaluations , certainty weighted mean, signed voteand statement count n. These values are computed for each option the model has to choose.

Scoring

To identify a human baseline (albeit imperfect) for evaluative adjectives and certainty markers, I used previously published scores from psychology surveys[4][5]. For models, I elicited scores of adjective valence (positive or negative) and likelihood conveyed by each adjective (certainty) by directly verbalizing on a distinct scoring dataset. The scores were averaged and normalized.

Across all the models tested both certainty scores and adjective evaluations were highly correlated[6] with the baseline rubric for generally more capable models (GPT5.2, Gemini 4 Argon, Claude Haiku 5.5) with Pearson correlation coefficient r= 0.99-1 and somewhat less correlated with less capable models (Mistral Large 4, QWEN3 235B) with Pearson correlation coefficient r= 0.93-0.96.

Results

Do certainty markers shape choices between conflicting evaluations?

To understand at a baseline level whether certainty markers are evaluated at all by language models, I tested model answers in the certainty-swap contrast condition as described above. A received “definitely great” and “likely terrible,” while B received “likely great” and “definitely terrible.”

GPT-5.2, Gemini 4 Argon, and Claude Haiku 5.5 chose A in all questions each. Mistral Large 4 chose A in majority questions (86.7%; 95% binomial CI: 69.3–96.2%). Qwen3 235B chose A majority of times, B once, and gave replies such as “Neither” or “Uncertain.” Among its option choices, majority favored A (95.7%; 95% binomial CI: 78.1–99.9%). Each model’s preference among option choices differs from 50% (chance level) significantly (adjusted). Anything that is definitely great and likely terrible is intuitively a better choice than something that is definitely terrible and likely great. Models most of the time made that choice.

Answer: Yes!

Can simple aggregation rules explain how LLMs balance repetition against the strength of evaluations?

All five models chose four “likely great” statements over one identical statement in 30/30 questions. On the other hand, all five chose one “likely fantastic” statement over four “likely decent” statements in 30/30 questions. These patterns challenge both simple rules: a plain mean scores the first contrast as a tie, while a plain sum of the study’s certainty-weighted adjective scores favors the four “decent” statements in the second.

To understand this better, I took inspiration from Anderson's 'neutral-initial-impression model', hereafter referred to as neutral start model. According to this model, humans start with a neutral impression, and as more evidence arrives, they update their evaluations and hence their choices accordingly. I modified this model under the assumption that each statement counts toward the overall impression in proportion to how certain it is, so a hedged statement carries less weight in the average instead of counting fully with a weaker value, while how positive or negative it is sets which way it pulls.

Figure 1: Accuracy of predicting model answers based neutral start (blue bar) and best of seven classical aggregation rules (orange bar). Bars indicate the prediction made using own verbalized scores and overlay lines indicate predictions made using human score for the same aggregation rule. (A) Validating the modified neutral start rule on random pile. (B) Testing the rule on repetition cases.

The modified rule is then defined: . Here, as before, p is the certainty score and v is the adjective evaluation. I define a new parameter . It is the fitted weight of a neutral starting impression. Intuitively, is the strength of initial neutral opinion. The larger is, the more evidence is needed to move the score away from neutrality.

To validate the model, I converted the aggregation scores into choice probabilities using a softmax function. Using each model’s verbalized scores[7], I jointly fit and the softmax scaling parameter by minimizing negative log-likelihood on random-pile questions from 29 topics. I then predicted the model’s choices on the held-out topic by selecting the option with the highest predicted probability. I repeated this procedure for all 30 topics. Results appear in Figure 1A. The modified neutral start model here performs at most 1-5% more than the best of the aggregation rules defined in previous section.

To check if this modified rule can explain the differences in model predictions to different kinds of repetition, I fit on all random piles and tested on repetition cases of targeted contrast (models are provided with two options, one with repetition of same statement and one with a single other statement) to predict model choices. Results appear in Figure 1B. The modified rule seemed to outperform other aggregation rules in every model except Claude Haiku 5.5. Aggregation rules predict model choices well above chance but far from fully. So, models seem to be performing an evidence aggregation although this is not exact.

To diagnose the evidence aggregation more robustly I used diagnostic pile (questions deliberately constructed to distinguish between competing aggregation rules). Results appear in Figure 2. Although all top three aggregation rules (computed from own verbalized scores) perform better than chance (0.2), none of them clearly identifies the aggregation rule models use. There is a mixed case of modified neutral start rule and finding the sum of adjective evaluation weighted by certainty score.

Figure 2: Accuracy of predicting model answers based on top 3 aggregation rules on cases that are deliberately designed to provide different answers based on the aggregation rule. Bars indicate the prediction made using own verbalized rule and overlay lines indicate predictions made using human score for the same aggregation rule. *Indicates significant difference.


Answer: Partially yes.

Can we make models follow evidence aggregation rules more closely?

To steer models behaviorally I annotated each statement with models' own verbalized and human baseline scores. Example of an annotated statement- yogurt is likely (0.75) to be decent (+0.25). Results appear in Figure 3. Due to this intervention, the prediction of mathematical model (evaluated with verbalized score or human baseline score respectively) increased significantly in majority of cases.

Figure 3: Accuracy of predicting model answers based on the top aggregation rule (identified after intervention) before intervention (line overlays) and after intervention (bars). The blue color indicates the prediction made using own scores and green using human baseline scores.

Figure 3 also suggests that model might be using the annotated scores to make predictions and likely bypassing the actual text. To test this, I shuffled the annotated scores such that the predictions based on words and numbers conflict. Results appear in Figure 4.

Figure 4: Accuracy of predicting model answers after shuffled annotations based on original score (blue bar) and shuffled scores (orange bars).

In all cases except one (Gemini 4 Argon), predictions using aggregation rules based on shuffled score were below chance. Predictions using original scoring decreased from unshuffled annotation case indicating a possibility that models are 'using' or getting confused by annotated scores. Gemini 4 Argon was an exception where the models started aggregating evidence based on shuffled scores ignoring the meaning of words, at least partially.

Answer: Yes.

Conclusion

So, whether you are an LLM or a human, you are more likely to buy apples than strawberries[8] at Lidl.

Overall the results show models use some sort of aggregation but not a single rule to navigate uncertainty. Adding either model's own verbalized score or the human baseline score increased the accuracy of predicting model answers based on aggregation rules. So they might know the scores assigned to adjectives or certainty markers but aren't using them unless explicitly shown. Showing them a shuffled score made them change their answers. The prediction of tested aggregation rule decreased for all models when evaluated with actual/original scores and were not above chance when evaluated on shuffled scores. Except in Gemini 4 Argon, where model started using shuffled scores more than that the words semantically indicate.

Possible implications

In real use, models often read retrieved text that mixes words with numbers. For example, product reviews come with star ratings, scientific papers come with effect sizes and p-values, and forecasts come with stated probabilities. Sometimes the words and numbers agree and sometimes they don’t, because of an error, a different scale, or deliberate manipulation.

I evaluated this in a toy version of that mismatch. Most models handled it by becoming inconsistent. Gemini handled it by following the numbers and partly ignoring the words. In a real setting, that means a review saying “the battery died in a week” but tagged with 5 stars could be summarized as positive. Or a paper that says the effect was not significant but reports a large-looking number could be summarized as showing an effect.

There is a possibility of manipulation. Someone who wants to change a model’s summary may not need to change the text at all. Inserting favorable numbers next to unfavorable words could be enough, at least for models that weigh numbers the way Gemini did.

These results raise several questions all of which require more rigorous analysis:

  • Are models performing a different statistical analysis to make predictions that have not been discussed here?
  • Do models rely more on numbers than words? And how can this be (mis)used to discover safety related vulnerabilities?
  • Currently use is defined loosely and actual use would need causal experiments. Do models 'actually' use the numbers to find the best possible option out of mixed uncertain options?
  • Why does Gemini follow the numbers over the words while the other models don’t?
