item.title: "Holy shit" graphs and how to get more of them
item.description:
We are likely in a situation where the most powerful models in the world are internal models, and, here's a key distinction, potentially even models that are never intended to be released to the public (i.e. a model designed to provide internal uplift on capabilities during training but that is not intended to be / not particularly suitable for commercial purposes.)

Internal-external information and capability gaps can distort both public and regulatory perception of frontier capabilities and dangers. If the internal frontier is three or six months ahead, such a gap is worrisome if the labs are close to automating various bottlenecks to increased capabilities development, like automating AI R&D.

Some ways of mitigating these visibility gaps and communicating the existing data we do have are implementable over the short term and confer minimal cost for many actors relative to the advantages of visibility for policymakers.

What is a "holy shit" graph?

Many of my intuitions about the coming impacts of AI are shaped by "Holy shit" graphs. The METR time horizon graph is one such graph, but has been discussed to death[1], so let's talk about another three:

Internal spending by OpenAI researchers (at API prices)

This spending graph is so bananas that when I try to google the source, The Gemini overview sometimes gets "AI token spending" and "Internal AI token spending by OpenAI researchers" confused and asserts that the thing I'm asking about could not possibly be true.

Epoch concludes:

Such rapid growth is probably unsustainable: if the recent growth in our preferred models continued for another year, annualized run rates would reach about $185 million for the median researcher and $2.3 billion for the 90th percentile researcher.

What the fuck.

General AI (as opposed to narrow AI) model revenues

This graph[2] shows the growth in frontier AI company revenues over time. It's unclear from the data labeling but this number is growing at 3-4x per year for the industry. To get a sense for the growth estimates, we can look at a prettier but more out of date graph from Epoch instead.


There seem to be some industry leader effects; Anthropic was growing faster when it was the second-highest company in revenue than now, and do note that this number may currently be slowing, and is itself an endogenous variable downstream of policy. Nevertheless, the industry as a whole is growing at a rate that would make it larger than the 2026 world economy by 2031-33. The point is not that this will continue forever, it's that if it doesn't stop continuing soon, the world must start looking very strange by the early 2030s, if not earlier.

Extent of AI R&D automation

It's hard to see from this graph, but it seems like it is currently taking about 15 months from a category to go from low single digits to fully saturated, and about seven months for the category to reach roughly the same level that the graph was at. This would seem to predict, again absent regulation, ~8 months from the end of the graph (6 months from now) to AL4-5 hitting ~99% and ~22 months from the end of the graph (20 months from now) for the AL5 category to hit 100%. Indeed, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark estimated back in the halcyon days of May 2026, a 60% chance that "an AI system powerful enough that it could plausibly autonomously build its own successor – happens by the end of 2028."

We can and likely should discount this from its source, but discounting it and the many related arguments all the way to "nope, not going to happen" seems hopeful.

I think communicating these "Holy shit" graphs, insofar as they are accurate, and we should have ways of verifying their accuracy externally, might be one of the most impactful pieces of communication the labs can give policymakers and the public.

Indeed, the accuracy of the first graph is weird. If we look back at the first few months of the graph, it would seem to imply that even though Codex launched in early 2025, it took until well into 2026 for Codex use to become widespread at the company. This is reasonable-ish speed of diffusion? But certainly non-obvious.


In any case, I'm not going to justify these claims here,[3] but Anthropic[4] reaching 100% AL5, and indeed even "only" substantial fractions of model R&D work being at AL5, seems like a four to five-alarm fire loss of control risk. This graph is a good starting point in evaluating the case that we are a couple of years away from full AI R&D on the default path, instead of 10 or more.

So it seems robust under many worldviews that independent evaluators and regulators being able to audit this information more comprehensively would be good thing. The graphs ought to be trustable, and indeed we should be cautious of those that are impossible to audit.


So what makes a "Holy shit" graph, in this definition? Three things:

0th: Your graph encodes a model of reality that is reasonably accurate, to your best understanding. Your graph being honest is not a pre-requisite for it going viral, but I will be very sad if you take this post as encouragement to make irresponsibly misleading graphs :(

  1. Sustained trend over a non-trivial number of data points, and the trend doesn't yet seem to be budging.
  2. Extrapolating out the trend naively gives crazy results.
  3. So there must be a trend break, surely, but the impacts of the trend break are likely to be severe as well.


I think the labs are sitting on a bunch of these data sources, and it would be good if we had more of them. Here's a few suggestions:


- Increased training metric transparency: Regularly updated[5] series showing number of current training runs above some FLOP threshold (potentially , in concordance with EU AI Act), FLOP count of largest active training run, FLOP count of largest ever training run.

- Increased deployment metric transparency: Time since end of training, total revenue breakdown for each model[6]

- Agent metrics: Current count, 99.9th percentile length session (actual max might fail to preserve privacy, but might still be an important indicator of a rogue agent)[7], number of websites


The high-level point is having a set of measurements which we can reference and which serve as high-level primary-source indicators of the 0th, 1st and 2nd derivatives of capabilities growth.

But insight into speed of diffusion also matters, I would argue for both understanding the mechanics of diffusion and for study of gradual disempowerment. Much has been written about gradual disempowerment [8], and indeed I think it's a policy area that is as important or more to understand as even the x-risk landscape. But much less has been written about how to operationalize it, though the GD paper authors do cite this as important follow-up work. Part of the reason that less work has gone into these metrics is that existing labor automation tools capture it meaningfully, but there are facets of the problem that go beyond economic and labor impacts. I'd love to see work done to measure every all three sections of the paper. Here are some thoughts:


Labor, relational and political


- Amount of time spent on claude.ai or chatgpt.com, averaged across every American[9] or across the whole globe.

- Amount of time spent on claude.ai or chatgpt.com, averaged across every American.

- Measurements of aggregate token output, and some translation of said token output to a "human-equivalent hours worked" concept.

- Percentage of Americans that have most of their political content or discussion come from a chat application or agent.


This could be you!

Are you an individual researcher, research organization or group working on alignment? Maybe you could make some "Holy shit" graphs with datasets that are already public or could be made public if requested?

If you're a grantmaker or manager, area worth thinking about?

I think METR and Epoch are, in important ways, highly cited in part because they make "Holy shit" graphs. It also seems important to me that these graphs have distinctive visual style and branding, and that they are either hand-crafted by humans or that their AI contributions are not highly visible; if the same graph was in some sense "equally good" but designed by the visual style of even Opus 5.5[10], many would disengage from the graph.

This does not mean that you should pivot away from the wonderful work that you are currently doing and go make "holy shit" graphs. I do think the number of useful "Holy shit" graphs is relatively small, maybe 20 or 50? And many of the best ones require a lab to publish the relevant data product. But the more general point I'm trying to gesture at is that investing in communicating your work legibly to your audience of choice is highly cost effective.[11] Maybe someone on your team should be making "Holy shit" graphs, or identifying future "Holy shit" graphs you could make, or in general investing in communicating your research memorably, legibly, and in a way that gets your organization's logo around the internet a few hundreds of thousands of times.

Note that though I think this work is on average net positive, I am arguing it is also a force multiplier for your work. If many people currently think your work is net negative, consider engaging effortfully with those arguments before making the cool graph.

    2. The sample size for the experiments was vanishingly small, with n=4 for some data points.
    3. The METR task suite systematically overestimated task length, as the participants took a surprisingly long time getting oriented on task basics.

    The first point is a fairly strong criticism, and the second one should make us worry about the measurement error of the task suite, but the third point I would argue has the opposite sign.     But in any case, if we're worried about the external validity of the experiment, METR has designed other graphs with comparable results. item.description:
This is what I have learned studying basic group theory. The ordering of the subjects might have a few oddities, but it's what makes the most sense to me. There are some of the definitions where the motivating reasons weren't properly explained in any of the textbooks I read, and I had to work them out myself; in the best case this post's justifications will be more intuitive, and in the worst case they'll be incorrect nonsense. The main textbook I followed was Álgebra Exemplar (Exemplary Algebra) by Sérgio Martins and Eduardo Tengan.

What is Symmetry?

Group theory is the study of symmetry.

A symmetry is usually defined as a transformation that leaves something unchanged. For example, the symmetries of this equilateral triangle are the (linear) transformations that take the triangle to itself. These are the rotations by [1] clockwise or counterclockwise, reflections about the axes shown above, and (trivially) the identity transformation.

We can be a bit more precise than "a function that leaves something unchanged". You have probably heard of the notion of an isomorphism, a bijection between two sets that respects some kind of structure. If there's an isomorphism between two sets, they are "the same" (isomorphic) regarding that structure, so that anything we can say about one transfers directly over to the other.

For example, in linear algebra, the structure of a vector space is set by the operations of vector addition and scalar multiplication. This means an isomorphism of vectors spaces is a bijection that preserves these operations: an invertible linear transformation.

A symmetry is an isomorphism from a set into itself. Symmetries let you see different perspectives from which you can look at the same structure, the degrees of freedom in its presence, the different possible implementations of its interface.

The symmetry maps of a vector space are the invertible linear transformations from the space to itself. We can pin down each vector in a vector space by introducing a basis; a symmetry map can be seen as a change of basis.

Groups and Subgroups

A group is an abstract representation of the set of an object's symmetries. The set of the triangle's 6 symmetry transformations is a group, called (for "dihedral group"). The set of all invertible linear maps from a vector space to itself is another group, called (for "general linear group").

Let's start by asking, if is a set and is the set of its symmetries, what properties should satisfy? Here are a few:

  • Isomorphisms are invertible, and their inverses should also be isomorphisms, because their whole point is that you can go back and forth between representations without losing information. So for any symmetry , its inverse should also be in .
  • Obviously if you don't do anything this preserves the structure, so the identity map, [2] such that for all , should be a symmetry; we'll require that .
  • If two operations and both preserve a structure, then applying first and then should not disturb it. This means the composition of all symmetries should also be in .

The definition of a group will be abstract, so that a single group can simultaneously represent the symmetry structure of many different sets. So a group is just a set , the identity and inverses are members of , and composition is a binary operation , with no explicit reference to another set whose symmetries represents.

We then need to guarantee that only the sets that can represent a set of symmetries will count as groups, by imposing axioms on and the operation . The following axioms are obviously always true when the operation is composition, and turn out to be enough:

  • Identity: composing with the identity does nothing, or there is an such that for all .
  • Inverses: applying a function then its inverse will put each element back where it started, or for every there is a such that .
  • Associativity: if you compose together the application of then then , it doesn't matter whether you first combine with or with , or for all .

So a group is any set with a binary operation that satisfies those axioms. We'll write the group operation as a product for short, so we write as , and repeated times as . An easy induction proof[3] shows that , so we can also write these as .

Note that the group operation doesn't have to be commutative, because neither does composition: in general. Some specific groups are commutative; they are often called abelian groups.

Then you'll need to restrict its symmetries to only the subgroup of that respects the inner product, not changing lengths or angles: the orthogonal transformations .

Examples

Let's look closer at the product in the triangle's symmetries . If we name the counterclockwise rotation , then is the other rotation and is the identity . If we name the reflection about the vertical axis , then , and multiplying by a rotation gives you another reflection. So the group's elements can be written as . The identity and rotations form a subgroup of , ². The identity and one of the reflections will also form a subgroup. If you count the elements of each of 's subgroups, you'll get 1, 2, 3 or 6. It is not a coincidence that these are the multiples of 6; we'll prove all subgroups must divide the side of their group.

Generalizing, -sided polygons for any have their own symmetry groups , with the identity, rotations and reflections. A vector space such as forms a group under vector addition. Its elements correspond to translations of n-dimensional Euclidean space. We usually represent Euclidean space by itself, fixing a point to be the origin; the difference between Euclidean space and is that Euclidean space should be symmetric under translation. This means you can only do vector operations on displacements between two Euclidean points, not on the points themselves, because the displacements are the same vector no matter where you put the origin, so they're invariant under translation of the space.

The integers , reals and complex numbers also make groups under addition which can represent translation. If you take out zero, the real numbers and complex numbers also form groups under multiplication. These multiplication groups can represent scaling transformations in a vector space.

Using the concept of homomorphisms, we can go back to our original notion of using groups to encode the symmetries of objects. An action of a group on a set is defined as a homomorphism , where is the group of bijections from to itself.

An action usually defines "the symmetries of " as , the embedding of . Of course, it's only an embedding of the entire group when is injective. Otherwise, has redundancies and we can represent 's symmetries by some other group that is actually isomorphic to . When is indeed injective, the action is called faithful.

Orbits and Stabilizer Subgroups

item.title: Important details in the leaked Anthropic draft AI bill
item.description:
There is a draft AI bill (discussed here, Politico reports it's being pitched by Anthropic) that has been making the rounds. I have some takes that I think differ somewhat from those I've been seeing so far in the AI-safety-adjacent discourse, centered around interpretation of specific portions that I think may be under-appreciated in how people are reading the bill. I walk through those here.

TL;DR

  • An explicit statutory path to block a model would probably make a federal block more likely, relative to current law
  • The draft includes provisions that seem to preserve significant federal authority to "block" AI labs (Section 12(a)(2))
  • The preemption section, as written, doesn’t preempt state suspension of models. If that is "fixed" other parts of the preemption provision would probably preserve a lot of state law AI claims, like public nuisance suits.

Scope

  • I'm working off the text here.
  • I'm primarily interested in questions like those raised here about whether this draft bill makes it harder for courts to block or restrict AI labs. The draft bill refers to a "blocking order" as "an order suspending the development, deployment, or internal use of a frontier model on the ground that the model presents an imminent enumerated risk". I think that is a good baseline for what it means for a court to "block" the actions of an AI lab. I have in mind here a slightly broader definition, something like "an order suspending development, deployment, or internal use".
  • I'm only considering the draft bill vs current federal law, not a comparison to something like the FRONTIER Act.
  • Nothing I say here is meant to suggest the draft bill is overall good or bad. I just think some of these details are being glossed over.

Details people may have missed

Statutory path to blocking

Courts can't block the actions of AI labs on their own initiative; they need a case in which that is an appropriate remedy. It isn't clear to me that there is a direct route to a federal cause of action for an AI system that poses a catastrophic risk under current law. There are definitely arguments that one could make under various laws, but courts may be hesitant to read existing law too broadly. A big impact I think a bill like this would have is that it would create specific statutory authority, approved by Congress, for a court to do some blocking. I think this is actually the predominant effect the bill would have on the likelihood of a federal block, and as a result I think it would increase, rather than decrease, the likelihood that a court would block actions by an AI lab (again, relative to status-quo).

The draft does impose some important limitations, such as the action needing to come from the Commerce Secretary (so a presidential administration that doesn't want to act is a big impediment), putting the burden on the Secretary, requiring de novo review at various stages, requiring a showing that a blocking order is the least restrictive option that addresses the risk, expiring a blocking order after 45 days, and barring consideration of evidence a lab hasn't seen.

Reasonable people can disagree on how the balance of these factors pans out. My read of the recent history of US federal courts is that standing is becoming a very relevant concern and plaintiffs with creative theories may face a more hostile environment, making an explicit statutory mechanism highly valuable. That inclination informs my take that the explicit federal route would be a pretty big deal.

Section 12(a)(2)

Section 12 deals with orders restricting the actions of AI labs. Section 12(a)(2) specifically disclaims effects on other laws:

No department, agency, or officer of the United States may suspend the development, deployment, or internal use of a frontier model under this Act except pursuant to an order entered or issued under this section. Nothing in this section affects authority under any provision of law other than this Act.

I think this would mean that the bill wouldn't substantially decrease the likelihood of a court blocking the actions of an AI lab under other federal statutes. This would also seem to cover executive agency action that doesn't need involvement of the courts as well.

Section 14(b)(1)

Section 14(b) is the preemption provision. As written, this includes Section 14(a)(1)-(3) in what is preempted, leaving out Section 14(a)(4) "suspension of models". This would seem to preempt parts of state laws like NY's RAISE Act or California's SB 53 to the extent they impose disclosure, evaluation, or incident-reporting obligations, but also allow state law activity on "suspension of models". It's unclear to me whether this is because there is meant to be a Section 14(b)(2) that addresses how preemption as applied to Section 14(a)(4) is meant to work, or whether (4) was left out of Section 14(b)(1) accidentally.

Section 14(a)(4) also includes the limitation that "This paragraph shall have no effect unless section 12 is enacted". Section 12 is the "blocking orders" section. This suggests to me that the drafters' intention is that preemption of "suspension of models" would only occur if there is also a federal route for this (under Section 12). That is very different from some prior advocacy of federal preemption of AI legislation (e.g. the 2025 Senate reconciliation bill "moratorium"), where the desire seems to be to lock-in a regime of relatively limited regulation. I think Section 14(d) and (e) and Section 15(c) also support this conclusion. Section 15(c) includes "It is the intent of Congress that State authority be displaced under section 14 only so long as the Federal requirements of this Act remain in force", which seems to suggest pretty strongly the goal here isn't to preempt for purposes of blocking regulation in general.

If we assume Section 14(b)(1) is updated to include all of Section 14(a)(1)-(4), I think Section 14(c)-(g) still preserve a lot of state law claims, such as public nuisance suits against AI labs. Section 14(a)(4) does include "judicial decree", while Section 14(c)(5) preserves state authority to apply its common law, so it isn't definitive. Arguably Section 14(e) would mean that ties go to the state.

Worth watching

  • Updated drafts may clarify how preemption is meant to work with regard to Section 14(a)(4).
  • Suncor (argued Oct. 5 at SCOTUS, awaiting decision) addresses preemption in the context of public nuisance suits against energy companies for their conduct relating to climate change. This is the route that Section 14 potentially leaves open.
  • Whether Section 12(a)(2) gets weakened or strengthened, and if any information comes out about how it's meant to function within the context of the draft bill.

item.title: Why I care about imperfect-recall games
item.description:
Lightly edited, partially by Opus 5.5, from a post on X.com

Why do I even care about imperfect recall games? Why do I have opinions on the Sleeping Beauty problem? It's a long story. I have a sketch of the connections between a number of areas: anthropics, decision theory, reinforcement learning, consciousness. But I don't have the full formal story yet.

Sleeping Beauty

What is the Sleeping Beauty problem? On Sunday someone flips a coin without telling you the result, and you go to bed. On Monday you wake up. If the coin was tails, you get memory-wiping drugs on Monday night, so when you wake up on Tuesday, you can't tell whether or not it's still Monday. If the coin was heads, on Tuesday you're told that it's Tuesday and that the coin was heads. [1] So when you wake up without being told anything, you don't know the coin: it might be heads or tails, it might be Monday or Tuesday, who knows? Well, what's the chance it's heads?

Some people say 1/2, some people say 1/3. I say 1/3. The basic 1/3 argument (from Elga 2000) is: it's equally likely that the coin is heads and it's Monday, and that the coin is tails and it's Monday (if you learned it was Monday, the coin would just be a fair coin). And also, it's equally likely that the coin is tails and it's Monday, and that the coin is tails and it's Tuesday (if you learned it was tails, nothing distinguishes the two days). So those three possibilities each get 1/3. But some people (famously Lewis 2001, "Sleeping Beauty: Reply to Elga") think that since 1/2 is clearly the right probability on Sunday, and you learn nothing new when you wake up, it should still be 1/2.

Can you even have credences about when and where you are?

But what are we doing here? How is "it's Monday" an event? Can we assign probabilities to things like "it's Monday" or "I am currently in the United States"? Aren't probabilities supposed to be about objective events, like whether the coin came up heads?

Well, now we get into interpretations of probability. Is probability about objective chances, like real frequencies in physics, where things go one way or another? Or is it about subjective credences: consistent beliefs, what people are willing to bet on? In the first case, objective chances, we could resolve these questions by asking a physicist. It takes a philosopher to untangle the second (Bayesian) approach, though.

I believe I am in the United States, and that it is October 2026, with high probability. Is that okay to have beliefs about? Yes. I can test both beliefs decently well. I can ask people around me what country it is, and what year and month it is. I can check clocks. So yeah, I can assign probabilities to my time and location.

In philosophy this is called a centered world (going back to Lewis 1979, "Attitudes De Dicto and De Se"). A centered world model says how the universe is (ideally the whole block universe across spacetime, although the physics gets weird there), and it also says which part of the universe is here and now. It's like, in a multiplayer video game, a centered world model wouldn't just say the state of the game, it would say which player you are.

And that's good for making predictions. How do you know, as a player, what you will see happen next, if you don't know which player you are? So if I'm assigning subjective credences to things, sure, why not to my own time and place?

Betting, and why CDT matters here

Okay, so what's the right subjective credence for "coin came up heads" in the Sleeping Beauty problem? I think it's 1/3. And that does make the betting odds work out. If you're going to bet on it, you should bet as if the probability is 1/3, since you will get two opportunities to bet if it's tails, and one if it's heads. (Concretely: if at every uncertain awakening you buy, for price , a contract paying $1 if heads, your expected profit is , which breaks even at .)

Now of course we could imagine a different bet, like a bet only offered on Monday in either case. But then being offered the bet tells you something new, it tells you it's Monday, so you should update your credences before deciding on the bet.

But wait, what does it mean to "bet as if the probability is 1/3"? Well, as long as the bet is about small amounts of money, it could mean pricing a contract that pays out $1 if the coin came up heads at about 33 cents. Of course, if someone offers you a bet, they might know something you don't, and that means you need to update your credences; but I'm imagining here that the bet is offered by a mechanical process, so there's nothing to worry about there.

But if your credence is 1/3, is it really correct to sell one of these contracts for $0.40, or buy one for $0.30? Is that really the obvious decision? We need a decision theory to decide this. Causal decision theory (CDT) is pretty simple and easy to work out here. It says yes: if your credence is 1/3, you should sell one of these contracts for $0.40 and buy one for $0.30, because the causal effect of doing so is positive in expected-value terms (assuming utility is differentiable in money with low curvature, so $1 isn't a lot, etc. etc.).

This really is specific to CDT. An evidential decision theorist who thirds would notice that her choice now is evidence about her choice at the other awakening, and would end up double-counting the tails world. Briggs 2010 ("Putting a Value on Beauty") shows that the coherent pairings are CDT with thirding and EDT with (a kind of) halfing. I've also argued that the various halfer positions are Dutch-bookable when combined with CDT, while CDT thirding isn't (Simple Dutch books versus Sleeping Beauty halfers).

Generalized thirding and local optimality

Okay, so CDT + thirding seems to do fine for bets. Let's generalize to generalized thirding (GT), terminology from Oesterheld and Conitzer; it's basically the Self-Indication Assumption (SIA). GT says: among the centered worlds compatible with your observations, assign each one probability proportional to the baseline physical probability of the corresponding uncentered world. So a world containing copies of your current information state gets weight proportional to times its physical probability. On physical grounds, the heads-world (uncentered) is exactly as probable as the tails-world (uncentered), but the tails-world contains twice as many copies of your information state (the one where you don't know if it's heads or tails, Monday or Tuesday), so it gets twice as much probability.

But how does this generalize? Is it really optimal to use CDT + GT? Well, kind of. If you set it up like a reinforcement learning problem, where you have a policy in an environment, and you have imperfect recall, and you take policy gradients, then CDT + GT is exactly the first-order stationarity (or, with the constraint that action probabilities lie in the simplex, KKT) conditions for the ex ante expected utility of the policy. See Piccione and Rubinstein 1997 on the absent-minded driver, my old post In memoryless Cartesian environments, every UDT policy is a CDT+SIA policy, and Tewolde, Oesterheld, Conitzer and Goldberg 2023, which relates (CDT, GT)-equilibria to KKT points of a polynomial maximization problem. KKT is a necessary condition for a local optimum, which is pretty close.

So if you're globally optimal, you're locally optimal. And if you're locally optimal, what you're doing is compatible with CDT + GT. But the converse is tricky.

The coffee shop problem

Imagine that you wake up on two different days, and each day decide to go to coffee shop A or coffee shop B. You'd really like to go to the same coffee shop both days. But all else being equal, you prefer shop A. Say you get 1 util for each day you go to A, plus 10 utils if you go to the same shop on both days. And your memory is wiped once, so when you make the decision, you don't know which day it is. Which one should you go to?

You should go to shop A, of course. But what if you for some reason thought you were likely to go to shop B on the other day? Say you think you go to B on the other day with probability . Holding that fixed (as CDT does), going to B gets you from coordination, and going to A gets you . So if , you should go to B, because coordinating with yourself matters more than going to the better coffee shop. So CDT + GT can end up always going to B, and that's stable. You could imagine an RL environment like this where the agent usually goes to B, and the policy gradients just keep reinforcing that.

That is annoying. It looks like CDT + GT is more of a necessary condition for rationality than a sufficient one. Well, why don't we require for rationality that your policy is the best one to commit to a priori? A priori, it would be great to commit to always going to A (12 utils), worse to commit to always going to B (10 utils), and even worse to randomize evenly between A and B (6 utils). [2]

Not everyone can be ex ante optimal at once

The problem is that not everyone can be optimal in this "ex ante" way simultaneously. Say there are two copies of Alice (or her memory is wiped once, either way), and each copy decides to go to shop A or shop B, which are equally desirable in themselves, but it's really important to Alice that both copies go to the same shop. Bob wants to go to whichever shop Alice goes to. Alice would rather not run into Bob, but she cares more about her copies meeting each other than about avoiding Bob.

Now try to make everyone ex ante optimal, meaning each player's policy is the best one to commit to given the others' policies. Alice has to send both copies to the same shop, deterministically; otherwise she risks failing to meet herself, which is really important. And as long as Alice always sends both copies to the same shop, Bob has to always go there too, otherwise he's being suboptimal. But now Alice is no longer optimal, because, holding Bob's policy fixed, it would have been better for her copies to coordinate on the other coffee shop. So there's no ex ante equilibrium. (This is in the spirit of Wichardt 2008, a classic counterexample showing Nash equilibria in behavior strategies needn't exist in games with imperfect recall; see also Tewolde et al. 2024.)

There might be a way to fix this, but it shows it's hard for everyone to be ex ante optimal. But there is an equilibrium where everyone is CDT + GT optimal: everyone goes to shop A all the time. Bob is taking his best action. When one of Alice's copies acts, that copy reasons that the other copy (and Bob) are both going to A, so she should also go to A, since breaking coordination with herself is worse than meeting Bob. That's CDT optimal. It's like a Nash equilibrium with three players, where two of them are copies of Alice with the same utility function, with the extra constraint that the two Alice copies use the same policy.

Newcomb's problem, simulations, and consciousness

What about Newcomblike scenarios? Take a version of Newcomb's problem where Omega predicts by simulating a copy of the CDT + GT agent, which sees exactly what the real agent sees. If the simulated copy one-boxes, Omega fills the opaque box with $1M, otherwise it leaves it empty; the transparent box always contains $1,000. People usually assume CDT two-boxes, but is this really true? The agent could reason that it might be the copy in the simulation. If it is the copy, it's very important for it to one-box, because that causes the real agent to eventually get $1M. And according to GT, there's a 50/50 chance it's the original or the copy. So one-boxing is worth about half of $1M in expectation, versus half of $1,000 for two-boxing, and it should one-box. That's also what it would have wanted to commit to originally.

But wait, what if the simulation isn't conscious? If the simulated copy isn't conscious, then the CDT + GT agent is going to assume there's no way it's the simulated copy. Since it knows it's not the simulated copy, there's no causal benefit to be had from one-boxing. So it two-boxes. That's the usual CDT analysis.

So it looks like the behavior of CDT + GT depends on whether it is a computational functionalist: whether it believes simulated copies of itself are conscious. Or maybe more precisely, it depends on which copies the GT probability rule counts as observers in the anthropic sense. But intuitively that's a lot like consciousness. It's not obvious why "anthropic observer" and "conscious being who can reason about anthropics" would even be different things.

We can even imagine an AI agent that uses CDT + GT and has a kind of prejudice: it thinks AIs running on GPUs can be conscious, but AIs running on water-pipe computers can't be. So now we make a version of Newcomb's problem for this agent, where the agent runs on GPUs and its simulated copy runs on water pipes. Because of its prejudice, it thinks there's no way it's the simulated copy running on water pipes, so there's no causal benefit to be had from one-boxing, so it two-boxes.

That's a problem for ex ante optimality. Before this whole Newcomb's problem instance, it would rather commit to one-boxing. But once it's in the room, it concludes it's in the real room (rather than a simulated version in a simulated room), and then it two-boxes.

Well, what if it has no such prejudices? It thinks all functional simulations of itself that Omega could use to predict it are conscious? That's pretty close to computational functionalism (CF). So a CDT + GT + CF agent might be able to act according to ex ante optimal policies. If it starts with the sort of policy it would have wanted to commit to, CDT + GT + CF will perhaps keep considering that policy rational. (This is basically the move in my memoryless Cartesian environments post, where Newcomb's problem is modeled by treating Omega's simulation as another copy of the agent. CF makes that modeling choice feel more natural from.)

Reinforcement learning

This relates to reinforcement learning again, because there are results suggesting RL behaves like CDT. For example, Bell, Linsefors, Oesterheld and Skalse 2021 show that value-based RL agents can't converge to policies that aren't ratifiable, i.e. that aren't optimal holding the policy itself fixed. So if you set up Newcomb's problem as an RL environment, RL algorithms are going to learn to two-box. The idea is that the environment could make two queries that run the agent's weights, but only one of them is an "action" for RL purposes; the other is just a computation run as part of the environment. Because of how RL credit assignment works, the agent gets credit for its effect on whether it one-boxes or two-boxes, but not for its effect on whether the opaque box is empty or full.

So reinforcement learning will learn to two-box. But maybe a more computational-functionalist version of RL would notice that there are two places where its weights are used to simulate it, even though only one is labeled an "action", and start thinking that it might be the other one, and that the other copy has causal effects on whether the box is empty or full.

(Why not just use FDT? Because FDT is defined in terms of logical counterfactuals, and those might not exist. It might be a fake concept with no formalization possible, or maybe a formalization is possible but no one has found one in over a decade because it's a hard problem. Even FDT's authors note that a full specification requires a theory of logical counterfactuals, see Levinstein and Soares, "Cheating Death in Damascus". FDT isn't math, at least not yet.)

Wrapping up
